introduction-the-heart-of-terraform.core: State is Terraform's memory: a JSON map from resource addresses in code to real-world IDs and attributes. Without it, Terraform couldn't know that aws_instance.web is i-0abc, couldn't detect drift or plan deletes. So state is critical infrastructure. It must be stored safely, shared, locked, backed up, and treated as sensitive.

first_principles.problem: A laptop with the only copy of terraform.tfstate is lost, and Terraform now wants to recreate production.
truths: Code says what; state says which.
derivation: Change it via **commands/blocks**, never by hand-editing.

analogy.title: A valet's ticket book
analogy.story: The ticket links your ticket number to a specific car in a specific spot; lose the book and nobody knows which car is yours.
analogy.breaks: Cars can be found by searching; recovering state means imports.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: See exactly which real object each address controls.

code.text:
terraform state list
# aws_instance.web
terraform state show aws_instance.web | head -3
# id  = "i-0abc123"

check.q: Why can't Terraform just query the cloud instead of keeping state?
check.a: Many resources can't be uniquely tied back to config without a stored mapping, and Terraform needs it to know what to update or delete.

remote-backends-and-locking.core: A backend decides where state lives and how it's locked. Remote backends (S3, GCS, azurerm, Terraform Cloud/HCP, PostgreSQL) give a shared, durable copy with locking so teams and CI collaborate safely. Bootstrapping the backend bucket itself is a chicken-and-egg problem, usually solved by a small separate stack or a one-off script.

first_principles.problem: Each engineer has a different local state file, and every apply fights the others.
truths: Shared state needs a shared store.
derivation: Bootstrap the backend in a **separate stack**.

analogy.title: A shared ledger in a bank vault
analogy.story: One authoritative copy, a sign-out sheet for editing, and nightly backups.
analogy.breaks: Vaults have guards; IAM must be configured explicitly.

code.text:
# backend.tf contains: terraform { backend "s3" {} }
terraform init -backend-config=env/prod.s3.tfbackend
# prod.s3.tfbackend
# bucket = "acme-tfstate-prod"
# key    = "network/terraform.tfstate"
# region = "us-east-1"
# use_lockfile = true

check.q: Why can't you use variables inside a backend block?
check.a: The backend is configured during init, before variables are evaluated, so it needs literal values or partial config files.

state-fracturing-layering.core: One giant state file means slow plans, huge blast radius and lock contention. Fracture state into layers that change at different rates and have different owners: foundation (accounts, networking), shared platform (clusters, databases), then applications. Each layer has its own state and pipeline, and lower layers expose outputs that upper layers consume.

first_principles.problem: A typo in an app's security group change shows up in a plan that also touches the production VPC.

analogy.title: Floors in a building with separate contractors
analogy.story: The foundation crew doesn't touch the office fit-out, and the fit-out can't move load-bearing walls.
analogy.breaks: Buildings are built once; layers redeploy independently all the time.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: App change plans in 20 s and can't touch the VPC.

check.q: What principle decides where to split state?
check.a: Group resources that share a lifecycle and owner, and keep dependencies flowing one way from lower to upper layers.

connecting-layers-remote-state-data-sour.core: Upper layers need lower-layer values such as the VPC ID and subnet IDs. The terraform_remote_state data source reads another stack's outputs directly, but it couples consumers to the producer's backend and grants them read access to its entire state, secrets included. Publishing values to a parameter store (SSM, Consul) or using tag-based data sources gives a narrower contract.

first_principles.problem: Granting the app team remote_state access to the network stack also exposes VPN pre-shared keys stored in that state.
derivation: Or **query by tags** with data sources.

analogy.title: Sharing a phone number vs your whole address book
analogy.story: Publishing just the number someone needs is safer than handing over the whole book.
analogy.breaks: Address books don't hold passwords; state files often do.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: App reads one value, never the network state.

check.q: What security drawback does terraform_remote_state have?
check.a: Readers need access to the whole state file, including any sensitive values, not just the outputs they consume.

drift-detection-reality-vs-code.core: Drift is when real infrastructure no longer matches code and state: console edits, other tools, auto-scaling, or deleted resources. `terraform plan -refresh-only` shows what changed in reality without proposing config changes, and a scheduled `plan -detailed-exitcode` (exit code 2 means a diff) turns drift into an alert. Decide per finding whether to revert to code or adopt into code.

first_principles.problem: A manually opened security group port sits unnoticed for months until an audit finds it.
truths: Plan compares code, state and reality.
derivation: Use **ignore_changes** for fields others own (e.g. ASG desired count).

analogy.title: Comparing the stock list with the shelves
analogy.story: A nightly stock-take finds missing or extra items before they become a problem.
analogy.breaks: Shelves don't change themselves; auto-scalers do legitimately.

example.title: Nightly drift job

code.text:
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -lock=false -out=drift.plan
rc=$?
if [ $rc -eq 2 ]; then
  terraform show -no-color drift.plan | ./notify-slack.sh "#infra-drift"
fi

example.outcome: drift as an alert, not a surprise.

check.q: What does exit code 2 from terraform plan -detailed-exitcode mean?
check.a: The plan succeeded and found changes, i.e. drift or pending changes exist.

importing-legacy-infrastructure.core: Click-ops resources can be brought under management without recreating them. Declarative `import` blocks (Terraform 1.5+) map an existing ID to an address and show up in the plan, and `terraform plan -generate-config-out` can draft the matching HCL. Iterate until the plan shows no changes, then the resource is safely adopted.

first_principles.problem: Hundreds of hand-built AWS resources must come under Terraform without downtime.
truths: State can map IDs to addresses.

analogy.title: Registering a stray dog
analogy.story: You don't buy a new dog; you microchip the one you have and record its details accurately.
analogy.breaks: Dogs don't have hidden settings; resources have many defaults to match.

check.q: Why is a zero-change plan the success criterion after importing?
check.a: It proves the config exactly matches reality, so applying won't modify or replace the adopted resource.

the-moved-block-declarative-state-refact.core: Renaming a resource or moving it into a module changes its address, and Terraform would destroy the old one and create a new one. `moved { from = ... to = ... }` blocks tell Terraform the object just changed address, so state is updated in the plan with no infrastructure change. Unlike `terraform state mv`, moved blocks are code-reviewed, applied by CI, and work for every module consumer.

first_principles.problem: Refactoring a flat config into modules plans to destroy and recreate a production database.
truths: Changed address looks like delete + create.
derivation: Check the plan says **'has moved to'**.
Keep moved blocks until **all consumers** upgrade.

analogy.title: A change-of-address card
analogy.story: The post office forwards your mail instead of declaring you gone and issuing a new identity.
analogy.breaks: Mail forwarding expires; leave moved blocks long enough for all consumers.

check.q: Why prefer moved blocks over terraform state mv?
check.a: They're versioned and reviewed in code, applied consistently by CI, and automatically apply for every consumer of a module.

sensitive-data-in-state.core: State stores resource attributes in plaintext, including generated passwords, private keys and connection strings, even when variables are marked sensitive (that only hides them in CLI output). So protect the state store itself: encryption at rest, tight IAM, no local copies, and keep secrets out of state where possible with managed secrets, ephemeral resources/values, or OpenTofu state encryption.

first_principles.problem: A developer with read access to the state bucket extracts the production DB master password.

analogy.title: A filing cabinet with copies of every key
analogy.story: Labelling keys 'secret' doesn't help if anyone can open the cabinet; lock the cabinet, or don't store the keys.
analogy.breaks: Cabinets are physical; state is copied to laptops and CI logs easily.

example.title: Let AWS own the password

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No password in state at all.

example.outcome: secrets kept out or locked down.

check.q: Does marking an output sensitive = true keep it out of state?
check.a: No, it only redacts it from CLI output; the value is still stored in state.
